title: Smile and Harvest
premise: Dominic Voss hosts a late-night radio show from a shuttered village station, taking calls from the recently dead who need one last message delivered. When the church bell that was melted down in 1911 rings across Hollowmere, the dead stop whispering and start demanding: the village's prosperity was built on a crime committed in 1974, when six families were drowned in the reservoir and their names erased. Dominic, whose own family signed the silence order, must return what was taken—the land deeds hidden beneath the studio floor—before the bell finishes ringing thirteen times and takes the living in place of the forgotten. In the end, Dominic broadcasts the truth to a village that cannot unhear it, gives the deeds back, and drowns with the dead rather than let his daughter inherit the debt.
about_author: Jude Brightwater is the pen name of a former small-town radio producer who spent a decade reading obituaries on air before turning to fiction. They write horror about the debts communities refuse to count.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Dominic Voss runs the overnight show 'Smile and Harvest' from a derelict studio, taking calls from listeners who died within the week—grief work he tells himself is charity. His daughter Wren keeps the generator running and counts the doors each night, a ritual she doesn't remember learning. POV: Dominic. Beat: eerie calm before the wrongness begins; establish love between father and daughter.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't
chapters.summary: The church bell—melted down in 1911, its bronze sold for shell casings—rings once at 3 a.m. Every phone line lights up at once, but the voices are older now, decades dead, repeating a single phrase: 'return what was taken.' Dominic checks parish records and finds pages razored out. POV: Dominic. Beat: dread arrives; the rules of the haunting reveal themselves as accounting, not vengeance.

chapters.title: Six Names Under Water
chapters.summary: Wren finds a child's shoe in the reservoir mud bearing a name no map records: Ellery Marsh. The village of Hollowmere was rebuilt higher after 1974, when the dam flooded the old low town—but six families supposedly relocated, not drowned. An elderly caller describes her own funeral. POV: Wren. Beat: grief curdling into suspicion; the past has a body count.

chapters.title: The Silence Order
chapters.summary: Dominic discovers his grandfather co-signed the 1974 settlement: hush money, forged relocation papers, and a clause binding descendants to secrecy. The deeds to the drowned lands sit in a lead box under the studio floor—the radio station was built deliberately over them. POV: Dominic. Beat: complicity; the horror is inherited, and he is the inheritor.

chapters.title: Callers Who Never Left
chapters.summary: The show becomes a tribunal. The drowned call in, polite and patient, each describing what was taken—not just land, but names, graves, the right to be remembered. One caller is Ellery Marsh, aged exactly as she died. She asks Wren, gently, if she'd like to hear her grandmother sing. POV: alternating. Beat: the dead are sympathetic; the living are the monsters.

chapters.title: Thirteen Rings
chapters.summary: The bell begins counting. Each night one more ring, and each ring erases something—a road, a photograph, a villager's memory of their own address. The councilman who profits from reservoir tourism organizes a vigil to 'pray it away.' It fails catastrophically. POV: Wren. Beat: escalation; time pressure made audible, the community fracturing.

chapters.title: What the Floor Keeps
chapters.summary: Dominic pries up the studio floor and finds the lead box—and his grandfather's suicide note inside it, confessing everything, never sent. The dead don't want money; they want broadcast. Truth spoken over the airwaves that carried the lie. But opening the box triggers the final countdown: three rings remain. POV: Dominic. Beat: moral climax approaching; confession as the only currency left.

chapters.title: The Last Broadcast
chapters.summary: Dominic goes live at midnight, reading the silence order, the names, the confession, while the councilman cuts power and villagers pound on the doors—Wren counts twelve of them, then thirteen. The generator holds. The bell rings its twelfth toll mid-sentence. POV: Dominic. Beat: climax; truth as exorcism, and the cost arriving on schedule.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Dominic carries the deeds to the waterline as the thirteenth ring sounds. The reservoir opens like a throat. He gives the papers to Ellery's hands, tells Wren to run uphill and never sign anything, and walks into the dark water among the six families, paying the family debt in full. POV: Wren. Beat: sacrifice; justice outside the law, paid personally.

chapters.title: Smile and Harvest
chapters.summary: A year later, Hollowmere has renamed its streets for the drowned, and the reservoir is being drained. Wren, sixteen, hosts the overnight show now. At 3 a.m. the phone rings once—a familiar voice, warm, saying only 'the lights are on, keep them counted'—and hangs up. She smiles through tears and signs off. POV: Wren. Beat: resolution; memory restored, grief transmuted into inheritance worth keeping.
